extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, regulators, policymakers, occupational safety professionals, public health researchers, and informed members of the public interested in asbestos law
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of legal, regulatory and policy standards governing asbestos production, use, management, disposal and liability across jurisdictions, including duties on property owners, workplace controls, national bans, international treaty obligations and compensation scheme criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete national bans on asbestos
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldwide, countries may adopt full bans on the use of asbestos; listed countries have banned the use of all types of asbestos (exemptions for minor uses permitted in some countries listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists numerous national bans with dates (e.g., Australia 31 December 2003; France 1997; UK 2000). Note that some bans allow limited exemptions for minor uses or for asbestos materials already in situ at time of ban. Enforcement and scope vary by country; check local implementing statutes/regulations for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basel Convention control of asbestos-containing waste
rubrics_metrics.description: Asbestos is listed under Annex I of the Basel Convention as a category of controlled waste; parties are required to prohibit export of hazardous wastes to parties that have prohibited import via the notification procedure in Article 13.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates an international obligation affecting transboundary movements of asbestos-contaminated wastes. Practical effect: exporters must not ship asbestos waste to jurisdictions that have prohibited import without following notification/consent procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to manage asbestos in non-domestic properties (UK Regulation 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dutyholders of all non-domestic properties must establish an asbestos register and a management plan and ensure a 'suitable and sufficient assessment' is carried out to manage the risk from asbestos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Non-domestic' is broadly defined (properties/structures where work is carried out). HSE emphasises 'Regulation 4 is a duty to manage, not [just] a duty to survey'. The asbestos register must state presence/absence of asbestos and management planning should identify actions to prevent exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk assessment factors for asbestos (HSE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk assessment involves assessing the type and condition of asbestos-containing materials and the likelihood of disturbance and exposure; human exposure potential depends on number of occupants, frequency/duration of use, and nature of disturbance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HSE uses a priority scoring tool combining material assessment and disturbance risk. Examples: intrusive maintenance increases risk; changing a light bulb presents far less risk than removing ceiling tiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building disturbance activity ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings/locations may be ranked according to disturbance activity: rare disturbance (e.g., little-used storeroom), low disturbance (e.g., office work), periodic disturbance (e.g., industrial use/vehicular movement), high disturbance (e.g., a frequently used fire door containing asbestos-insulating boards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ranking informs prioritisation in management plans and whether measures like removal, containment, labelling or simple access controls are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management outcomes identified by risk assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcomes of risk assessment can include urgent removal, removal/encasement of unsuitable materials, minor repairs, or labelling and provision of information as sufficient controls to avoid significant health risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of outcome depends on material condition and disturbance likelihood. For low-use areas, keeping a door locked and attaching a warning notice may suffice; high-risk materials typically require removal by licensed contractors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensed contractors and controlled removal for high-risk asbestos products
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of high-risk asbestos products (e.g., thermal insulation) must be carried out under controlled conditions by licensed contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HSE provides guidance on which products require licensing and maintains lists of licensees. Failure to use licensed contractors for work that requires a licence is a regulatory breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement for workers who may encounter asbestos
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a legal requirement that all who may come across asbestos in their day-to-day work must be provided with the relevant asbestos training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training must be appropriate to the role (recognition, management, safe working practices). This requirement is part of employers' duties under the Control of Asbestos Regulations and related workplace health and safety law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for non-licensed asbestos work (Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some non-licensed asbestos work now requires notification and additional management (e.g., record keeping and health surveillance) after the 2012 Regulations transposing EU Directive changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are 'relatively minor' changes but mean some previously non-notifiable work must now be notified to authorities and managed with formal records and surveillance; consult the statutory instrument text and HSE guidance for which activities are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: No assumed safe exposure threshold for asbestos (HSE position)
rubrics_metrics.description: HSE does not assume any minimum threshold for exposure to asbestos below which a person is at zero risk of developing mesothelioma; any threshold, if it exists, must be at a very low level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This position influences regulatory conservatism in exposure controls and supports policies aimed at minimising exposure to the greatest practicable extent rather than relying on a 'safe' level.

rubrics_metrics.name: National statutory bans and prohibitions (manufacture/import/use) as legal instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries implement asbestos prohibitions via national statutes and regulations (examples: The Asbestos (Prohibitions) Regulations 1985 for UK blue/brown asbestos; Asbestos (Prohibitions) (Amendment) Regulations 1999 banning white asbestos in parts of UK; various national laws cited for other countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific regulatory instruments set the legal scope and effective dates of bans; practitioners must consult the up-to-date national legislation/regulations for compliance requirements and any transitional provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asbestos content threshold for regulation or ban (example: South Korea 0.1%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions use quantitative thresholds for asbestos content to trigger regulatory controls or bans (South Korea banned manufacture/import/sale/storage/transport/use of substances containing more than 0.1% asbestos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds determine whether products/substances fall within regulatory prohibitions; testing and certification may be required to demonstrate compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling, warnings and standards for asbestos-containing products (India examples: IS standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: National standards and guidance may require pictorial warnings, labeling and specific safe-usage guidelines (India: IS 11769 Parts 1–3 for safe usage; IS 12081 pictorial warning; IS 11451 occupational exposure requirements; IS 11768 waste disposal procedure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such standards set manufacturer and workplace obligations for warnings, packaging and disposal procedures. The page notes lack of enforcement in some settings, which affects real-world protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waste disposal and export controls for asbestos-containing materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Asbestos-containing waste is controlled (e.g., under Basel Convention and national hazardous-waste rules) and export/import may be prohibited or subject to strict notification and consent procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper waste classification, containment, documentation and adherence to international and national waste laws are required; failure to comply can lead to cross-border legal and environmental obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation periods and the 'time of discovery' rule in asbestos litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most countries have limitation periods to bar actions taken long after causes of action; some jurisdictions (e.g., Australia) amended limitations to start from time of discovery rather than accrual due to long disease latency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because asbestos-related diseases have long latency, the choice of limitation rule (discovery vs accrual) critically affects whether claims are time-barred. Practitioners need to check national limitation statutes and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latency of asbestos-related diseases as a legal factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Long latency (mesothelioma: often 20–50 years; other diseases 10–30+ years) is a central issue in civil litigation and compensation schemes because exposure may predate manifest disease by decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Latency affects causation proof, apportionment of liability across multiple employers/worksites, and statutory limitation considerations; courts and regulators adapt rules and evidentiary approaches accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation scheme eligibility criteria and categorisation (Asbestos Relief Trust model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief trusts/compensation schemes set eligibility categories and criteria (example: ART categories ARD1–ARD4 for asbestosis/pleural thickening, lung function impairment, asbestos-related lung cancer, mesothelioma) and require claimants to show exposure to funders' operations and a compensable disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides ART payout averages (R40,000; R80,000; R170,000; R350,000 for ARD1–4) and describes projections and success rates. Trust deeds specify evidentiary and exposure requirements; schemes may limit double recovery and have closing dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties, offences and transitional exemptions (example: South Africa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some national regulations create criminal offences and penalties for acquisition, processing, manufacture or distribution of asbestos products after prohibition, while allowing limited transitional exemptions (e.g., grace period to clear stock, imports for research/disposal under strict conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties can include fines and imprisonment (South Africa example: fine not exceeding R100,000 and/or imprisonment under ten years). Transitional provisions and exemption procedures are common; compliance requires awareness of deadlines and registration requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental and international listing and consent procedures (Rotterdam Convention/PIC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing asbestos under international instruments (e.g., Rotterdam Convention Prior Informed Consent list) triggers obligations on trade in hazardous chemicals; national positions (support or opposition) affect whether listing occurs and hence international trade controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents political contestation (e.g., India opposing PIC listing in 2017). Practitioners should monitor treaty processes because international listing changes import/export regulatory burdens and manufacturers' disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectoral and product-specific regulatory carve-outs and permitted specialized uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where general bans exist, jurisdictions may permit asbestos or asbestos-containing products for specialized uses (examples: Canada allowed certain specialised uses such as in nuclear facilities; some countries exempt minor/legacy uses or in-situ materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulated exceptions often come with strict controls, narrow scope, and administrative conditions; users must verify whether their product/use qualifies for an exemption and comply with any special registration, labeling or disposal requirements.
